books.section: Topic 9.3 The End of the Cold War
Prosperity and a New World Order (1988-2000)

rationales.A: Background: containment was the debate of the Cold War. With the Soviet Union gone, there was no communism left to contain in Europe.
rationales.B: Background: trade with Latin America was debated in the 1990s, but the passage's interventions raised a question about using force, not trade.
rationales.C: No serious debate asked the United States to give up its Security Council seat. The passage is about acting abroad, not leaving the United Nations.
rationales.D: The account lists American interventions in the Gulf, Somalia, Bosnia, and Kosovo, and says each crisis raised the question of whether to act.
rationales.general:
1. First, notice what ended: the rivalry that had set the terms of every foreign-policy debate.
2. Background: during the Cold War, the central question was how to contain communism.
3. The account says that question was gone by 1991, yet American forces still went abroad again and again.
4. So the debate shifted from whether to oppose communism to whether to use American power to stop suffering or stay out.
Remember: when the old question disappears, look for the new question the same events keep raising.

stimulus.source_note: Secondary account paraphrased from the grounding books (Barron's Premium 2027 Ch. 11; 5 Steps 2024 Ch. 29).
stimulus.text:
Paraphrase of a secondary account: When the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, the United States stood alone as the world's only superpower. The long rivalry that had shaped every American foreign-policy choice since 1945 was gone. In the 1990s, American forces fought Iraq in the Persian Gulf in 1991, joined a humanitarian mission in Somalia in 1992, and led NATO bombing campaigns in Bosnia in 1995 and in Kosovo in 1999.

At the same time, former Communist states in Eastern Europe opened their economies to world markets, and new trade agreements linked more countries together. No rival power now stood in the way of American action, and each new crisis raised the same question: whether the United States should act abroad or stay out.
